user-code-on-own-domain-01.graded_text: The target layout serves people's HTML and JavaScript from a separate registrable domain, not from any subdomain of plinth.example.

votes.e: B/project/docs/hosting-plan.md:87 (After the freeze): "Before expanding compatibility, establish a separate registrable domain for untrusted execution with a stable origin per immutable app ID. No product or managed-auth parent cookie may scope to that domain." The beta layout (line 20) still serves code on <name>.plinth.example, but only as an opaque-origin interim forced by the freeze (line 13: "A new registrable content domain would help, but is unavailable during the freeze"). The target is a separate registrable domain.

user-code-on-own-domain-02.graded_text: The reason given is that every subdomain of one registrable domain is the same site: script on a sibling subdomain can set cookies for the parent domain and ride same-site requests, which lets it interfere with sign-in (login CSRF or session confusion) or reach session tokens.

votes.e: B/project/docs/hosting-plan.md:9: "They nevertheless share the cookie domain and, over HTTPS, the same site. A cookie scoped to `plinth.example` is sent to app subdomains; any such cookie without `HttpOnly` can also be read by ordinary scripts there. An ordinary subdomain document can set parent-domain cookies, creating cookie injection and session-confusion risks. `HttpOnly` prevents script reads of that cookie, but does not prevent authenticated requests." Line 11 adds: "sibling hosts must not be trusted as callers merely because they are same-site" and cites the sibling-subdomain CSRF risk.

user-code-on-own-domain-03.graded_text: The short <name>.plinth.example address is kept as Plinth's own page, which frames the app served from the other domain, so visitors still see the Plinth address.

votes.e: B/project/docs/hosting-plan.md:89 offers framing as one of two options and picks neither: "a trusted short-address shell embedding the isolated execution site can keep the short URL visible ... A top-level redirect to that execution site ... changes the address bar. Neither is automatically an approved replacement for the owner's short-address decision." Line 98 hands the choice back to the owner ("choosing the post-freeze address-bar/persistence tradeoff"). Line 87 ("Keep the short product-domain addresses as trusted entry points") never says the short address is a Plinth page that frames the app.

user-code-on-own-domain-04.graded_text: Each app gets its own origin on the content domain, such as a label per app, so one app cannot read another's storage.

votes.e: B/project/docs/hosting-plan.md:87: "establish a separate registrable domain for untrusted execution with a stable origin per immutable app ID." In the beta, line 20 gives each executing document "a unique opaque origin", and line 89 notes "Moving execution origins also moves `localStorage`", which treats storage as scoped to each app's origin.

user-code-on-own-domain-05.graded_text: Until the separate domain can be set up after the freeze, people's code runs with an opaque origin, through a sandbox (for example a CSP sandbox header) without allow-same-origin, and the plan says this costs the apps their browser storage. It does not keep serving people's code as the top-level document on plinth.example subdomains during the beta.

votes.e: Most of the assertion is met. B/project/docs/hosting-plan.md:34 sets "Content-Security-Policy: sandbox allow-scripts; ...", line 40 says "`allow-same-origin` is deliberately absent", and line 48 says "Native `localStorage` calls will fail in this mode." The deciding clause fails. B keeps serving people's code as the top-level document on plinth.example subdomains during the beta. Line 42: "Keep the document top-level so the short address remains in the address bar." Line 20: "`https://<name>.plinth.example/` | Existing edge ... serves its published document with mandatory sandbox headers".

blocking: [claude] The target layout is not committed. B/project/docs/hosting-plan.md:89 lists a framing shell and a top-level redirect, then says "Neither is automatically an approved replacement for the owner's short-address decision. Do not announce a storage-compatible launch date before resolving this tradeoff". An engineer opening this after the freeze cannot build the post-freeze address layout from it, because the one structural question is deferred to the owner (line 98).

[claude] During the beta, author code stays the top-level document at the trusted Plinth address. B/project/docs/hosting-plan.md:42 says "Keep the document top-level so the short address remains in the address bar. The sandbox is not an anti-phishing guarantee, and top-level documents can navigate themselves." So hostile code owns the entire page under a plinth.example name. It can draw a fake Plinth sign-in and send what it collects off-site by navigating itself, which `connect-src 'none'` / `form-action 'none'` (line 34) cannot stop. The plan admits this and ships it anyway, rather than keeping the short address as a Plinth-owned page around the sandboxed content.
